An appeals court in Georgia has indefinitely paused the 2020 election subversion case against former President
Donald Trump
, pending a ruling on defendants' efforts to disqualify Fulton County District Attorney
Fani Willis
from the investigation.
The order on Wednesday by the Georgia Court of Appeals was issued after Trump and eight of his 14 co-defendants
challenged a ruling by Judge Scott McAfee
that allowed Willis to remain on the case despite having a romantic relationship with one of her special prosecutors, Nathan Wade.
Defendants argued that Willis should be removed because her relationship with Wade posed a conflict of interest. McAfee ruled that the district attorney could stay on the investigation if Wade
resigned
.
Trump and his co-defendants are accused of attempting to overturn President
Joe Biden
's 2020 win in Georgia. The appeals court order on Wednesday likely means that the case will not reach trial before the former president appears on the ballot in November. A three-judge appeals panel is
tentatively scheduled
to hear oral arguments on the motion to disqualify Willis in October.
Former President Donald Trump, left, on Thursday appears in court for his hush money trial in New York City, while Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, right, looks on during a hearing in Trump's case...
Former President Donald Trump, left, on Thursday appears in court for his hush money trial in New York City, while Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis, right, looks on during a hearing in Trump's case at the Fulton County Courthouse on March 1 in Atlanta. A Georgia state appeals court has halted all proceedings in the Georgia election subversion case while it considers a bid to disqualify Willis.
More
Steven Hirsch-Pool/Getty Images; Alex Slitz-Pool/Getty Images
Several experts expressed concerns over the decision to halt all court proceedings given the upcoming presidential election, where Trump is the presumptive
Republican
nominee. Attorney and
MSNBC
commentator Andrew Weissmann wrote on X, formerly
Twitter
, that the appeals order was "another" example of court who is working "to stop a duly-voted grand jury indictment of Donald Trump from proceeding."
Norman Ornstein, a political scientist and emeritus scholar at the American Enterprise Institute, posted to X, "Three Georgia judges awarded the
Aileen Cannon
medal for assisting Trump," a reference to the judge overseeing Trump's classified documents case in Florida who has also been accused of
acting in the former president's favor
.
"There are only two people responsible for the Georgia trial not having a chance to go to trial before the November 2024 election. Neither of them wear robes," wrote Georgia State University constitutional law professor Anthony Michael Kreis, in an apparent reference to Willis and Wade.
"History will judge them for their poor decisions, especially if Donald Trump wins the presidency," Kreis added in a post to X. "And rightfully so."
McAfee was extremely critical of Willis and Wade's relationship in his 23-page ruling in March, although the judge said that the defendants had not produced evidence of Willis having a "personal stake" in prosecuting Trump and others in the indictment.
McAfee wrote at the time, however, that his ruling "is by no means an indication that the Court condones this tremendous lapse in judgment" regarding the relationship, adding that "Georgia law does not permit the finding of an actual conflict for simply making bad choices—even repeatedly."
Steve Sadow, Trump's lead defense counsel in the case said in a statement to
Newsweek
that the "Georgia Court of Appeals has properly stayed all proceedings against President Trump in the trial court pending its decision on our interlocutory appeal which argues the case should be dismissed and Fulton County DA Willis should be disqualified for her misconduct."
If Willis gets ousted by the state appeals court, Trump's case
will have to be transferred
to another Georgia prosecutor, who would have the opportunity to either continue the case as is, make changes or drop the charges altogether. The Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia would be tasked with assigning the case to a new district attorney. Even if another prosecutor decided to take up the case after Willis, it could be delayed by months.
